paper.title_en: Using two-photon interference to perform ultrahigh-precision timing measurements: the origins of the Hong-Ou-Mandel effect
paper.abstract_en: In this paper, I recount the early experiments leading to the observation of the two-photon interference phenomenon commonly referred to as the "Hong-Ou-Mandel effect," observed in 1987 at the University of Rochester by Chung Ki Hong, Zhe-Yu Ou, and Leonard Mandel, and now widely used for quantum technologies. I show that Mandel and his collaborators originally designed their experiment not to probe the nonclassical properties of radiation, as one might think, but to perform ultrahigh-precision timing measurements on photon pairs produced through a nonlinear optical process, namely spontaneous parametric down-conversion. More broadly, I argue that the Hong-Ou-Mandel experiment resulted from the convergence of three distinct lines of research: nonlinear optics, the quantum properties of radiation, and, more unexpectedly, the foundations of quantum mechanics. Within this framework, I bring to light the work of physicists whose names do not appear in the acronym "HOM," but whose contributions proved crucial to the demonstration of two-photon interference-notably Stephen Friberg and Rupamanjari Ghosh within Mandel's laboratory, Yanhua Shih and Carroll Alley at the University of Maryland, and John Rarity and Paul Tapster in England.
